newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania revises budget to IMF praise.
newsitem.headline: Romania revises budget to IMF praise.

text.p: Romania took a key step towards securing fresh IMF credits on Wednesday by sticking to an approved deficit level in a revised budget.
A senior International Monetary Fund official responded by praising the government's reforms.
Finance Minister Mircea Ciumara said the budget had received approval in principle from the centrist cabinet after a session on Tuesday extending well past midnight.

He said the meeting had channelled more funds to the social sphere while other ministers had agreed to reductions to meet the IMF's demand to maintain the deficit at 4.5 percent of gross domestic product.

"The budget has been approved and the deficit stays at 4.5 percent of GDP," Ciumara said by telephone. "There have been increased allocations for the Health, Education and Labour ministries. All others have been subject to cuts."
The chief IMF negotiator for Romania, Poul Thomsen, praised the government's reform efforts and announced an agreement to extend the country's external debt ceiling by $500 million to $3.7 billion.

But he said more effort was needed to restructure loss-making industries and farms. And he sidestepped reporters' questions on whether he would recommend the IMF board release the second of five $86 million credits.
"As far as macro-economic policies are concerned, developments have been very positive. They are exceeding expectations," Thomsen said.
He said he had to return to Washington and "convince my colleagues that we have an agreement, which is a good agreement and I expect the Board to discuss it in early September".

Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's coalition of Christian Democrats, Social Democrats, Liberals and members of Romania's Hungarian minority launched reforms earlier this year after ending seven years of leftist rule in the 1996 elections.

Ciumara said budget calculations had taken into account lost revenue equivalent to $47 million for wage indexation agreed with trade unions and a further $82 million for maintaining subsidised electricity prices through the winter.

Ciumara had said on Tuesday, before the budget was approved, that the government would not guarantee for this year a deal to build nearly 100 combat helicopters in Romania with a U.S. firm as part of efforts to limit foreign borrowing.
Further unexpected constraints came from flooding which damaged houses in various regions and threatened what had earlier been forecast to be a bumper grain harvest.
Approval of a new budget was one of the principal IMF demands for release of the second credit under a $430 million, 13-month standby arrangement.
Others included renewed efforts to bring down monthly inflation, due to fall below two percent in July after hitting 30 percent in March owing to price liberalisation.
The pace of privatisation and restructuring inefficient communist-era enterprises were also key issues.
Ciumara, who had previously admitted that revenue from sell-offs was low, said he hoped "privatisation will accelerate in the months ahead...I am relying a great deal on this money."

Ministers have also criticised delays in restructuring or shutting down inefficient plants and farms. The government earlier this year issued a list of enterprises to be closed but little has been done to carry out the plan.
